title: Nvidia and Dell back AI cloud startup Volta at a $2.4bn valuation
excerpt: AI cloud startup Volta has raised $300m and lined up $5bn in financing at a $2.4bn valuation, backed by a16z, Altimeter, Nvidia, and Michael Dell.
content_html:
A new company wants to be the one that pays for everyone else’s AI chips. Volta Infra Holdings has raised $300m in venture funding and lined up a further $5bn in financing to help a broader range of tech firms afford Nvidia’s costly hardware, in a round that values it at $2.4bn.

The raise was co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and Altimeter Capital, with Nvidia and Michael Dell also taking part.

Volta’s pitch is a financing problem dressed as a cloud company. Its founders argue that only the biggest firms with the strongest balance sheets can afford the upfront cost of cutting-edge chips, and Volta wants to spread that cost so smaller labs can compete.

The model places Volta among the neoclouds, the wave of GPU-focused providers renting out AI compute, though its emphasis is as much on the money as the machines. A $5bn financing pool, arranged by the asset manager Azora from a mix of banks, is meant to bankroll its customers.

The company was founded this year by Ricard Boada and Sofia Gumuzio, both former executives in Brookfield’s infrastructure business.

‘We saw a massive opportunity and a massive gap in the market,’ Boada, now chief executive, said.

That background is the pitch. Building AI clouds has become as much a problem of power contracts, project finance, and bank relationships as of servers, and Volta’s founders come from that world rather than from software.

It is not starting small. Volta says it has already signed a $10bn, six-year contract to supply cloud capacity to a leading AI developer it declined to name, a marquee deal for a firm only months old.

That contract will run partly on borrowed ground. It is to be delivered with Bitdeer, a bitcoin miner turned data-centre operator, using a 133-megawatt site in Norway, with further sites planned in Texas and Wyoming.

The Bitdeer tie-up fits a wider shift. Bitcoin miners, sitting on cheap power and ready-built sites, have become unlikely landlords to the AI boom, repurposing infrastructure built for one gold rush to serve the next.

There is a European thread here, too. The first big site sits in Norway, and the founders came out of infrastructure investing rather than pure tech, a reminder that the AI buildout is not only an American story.

Power is the real constraint, and Volta has been securing it. The company says it has locked up a gigawatt of capacity in the near term, enough to power hundreds of thousands of homes, and is aiming for several gigawatts by 2030.

Volta is one of many trying to grease the same wheels. Nvidia itself has offered startups compute now and payment later, and Broadcom, Apollo, and Blackstone have lined up to fund chips for Anthropic.

Nvidia’s fingerprints are all over this market. The chipmaker has topped $40bn in AI equity bets this year and has discussed backing hundreds of billions of dollars in chip purchases for OpenAI, blurring the line between supplier and financier.

That blurring worries some. Critics call the arrangements circular, an interconnected web in which suppliers help fund the customers who buy their products, a structure that could magnify losses if AI demand falls short of the hype.

Even Volta’s backers had been sceptics. Andreessen Horowitz had largely avoided neoclouds and data-centre startups, but was won over by the founders’ record in financing projects and securing power, according to managing partner Raghu Raghuram.

Dell will act as a technology partner, supplying gear to Volta’s sites and adding another established name to its roster. Success, Raghuram said, would depend on mastering ‘the financial complexities of building and operating new clouds and selling to customers’.

Not everyone will survive the boom. ‘There’s going to be so many dead bodies and so much consolidation eventually,’ said Altimeter’s Jamin Ball. Volta is betting that its banker relationships and blue-chip partners are what keep it upright when the tide turns.

content_html_zh:
一家新公司希望成为为其他所有人的人工智能芯片付费的公司。 Volta Infra Holdings 已筹集 3 亿美元风险投资，并准备再融资 50 亿美元，以帮助更广泛的科技公司买得起 Nvidia 昂贵的硬件，本轮融资估值为 24 亿美元。

此次融资由 Andreessen Horowitz 和 Altimeter Capital 共同领投，Nvidia 和 Michael Dell 也参与其中。

Volta 的宣传是伪装成云公司的融资问题。 其创始人认为，只有拥有最强大资产负债表的最大公司才能承担尖端芯片的前期成本，而 Volta 希望分摊该成本，以便较小的实验室能够参与竞争。

该模型将 Volta 置于新云之中，即以 GPU 为中心的提供商出租人工智能计算的浪潮，尽管它的重点与机器一样重要。 资产管理公司 Azora 从多家银行中安排了一个 50 亿美元的融资池，旨在为其客户提供资金。

该公司由 Ricard Boada 和 Sofia Gumuzio 今年创立，两人都是布鲁克菲尔德基础设施业务的前高管。

现任首席执行官博阿达表示，我们看到了巨大的机遇和巨大的市场缺口。

那个背景就是球场。 构建人工智能云已经成为一个与服务器问题一样的电力合同、项目融资和银行关系问题，而 Volta 的创始人来自这个世界，而不是软件界。

这不是从小事开始的。 Volta 表示，它已经签署了一份价值 100 亿美元、为期六年的合同，为一家领先的人工智能开发商提供云容量，该开发商拒绝透露姓名，而这对于一家公司来说只是几个月前的一项重大交易。

该合同将部分在借用的土地上运行。 该项目将与 Bitdeer 一起交付，Bitdeer 是一家由比特币矿工转变为数据中心运营商的公司，使用挪威的一个 133 兆瓦的站点，并计划在德克萨斯州和怀俄明州建设更多站点。

Bitdeer 的合作适合更广泛的转变。 比特币矿工坐拥廉价电力和现成场地，不太可能成为人工智能热潮的房东，他们重新利用为一次淘金热建造的基础设施，为下一次淘金热服务。

这里也有欧洲的线索。 第一个大型站点位于挪威，创始人来自基础设施投资而不是纯粹的技术，这提醒人们，人工智能的建设不仅仅是美国的故事。

电力是真正的限制因素，而 Volta 一直在确保这一点。 该公司表示，短期内已锁定 1 吉瓦装机容量，足以为数十万家庭供电，并计划到 2030 年实现数吉瓦装机容量。

沃尔特（Volta）是众多试图为同样的轮子加油的人之一。 英伟达本身已经为初创公司提供了先计算后付款的服务，博通、阿波罗和黑石也已排队为 Anthropic 提供芯片资金。

英伟达的足迹遍布这个市场。 这家芯片制造商今年在人工智能股票上的投资已超过 400 亿美元，并已讨论支持 OpenAI 购买数千亿美元的芯片，模糊了供应商和金融家之间的界限。

这种模糊让一些人感到担忧。 批评者称这些安排是循环的，这是一个相互关联的网络，供应商帮助为购买其产品的客户提供资金，如果人工智能需求达不到宣传的水平，这种结构可能会扩大损失。

甚至沃尔特的支持者也对此表示怀疑。 据管理合伙人 Raghu Raghuram 表示，Andreessen Horowitz 基本上避开了新云和数据中心初创公司，但被创始人在融资项目和确保权力方面的记录所吸引。

戴尔将作为技术合作伙伴，为 Volta 的站点提供设备，并在其名册中添加另一个知名品牌。 拉古拉姆表示，成功将取决于掌握“构建和运营新云以及向客户销售的财务复杂性”。

并不是每个人都能在繁荣中幸存下来。 “最终将会有如此多的尸体和如此多的整合，”高度计的贾明·鲍尔说。 Volta 认为，当形势发生转变时，其银行家关系和蓝筹合作伙伴将使其保持稳定。
